title: Exceptional brain and ecological diversity in the earliest snakes.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed the Harvard Dataverse record (CC0 licence, 4 open files: README, SD2_Phylogeny.zip 42.6 MB, SD3_BrainEvol.zip 7.6 MB, SD4_Lifestyle.zip 2.7 MB). Downloaded and unzipped SD3 and SD4. SD3: 60 landmark files (.fcsv, 6 landmarks each on the front brain region) and SPECIES_CLASSIFIERS.csv with 60 rows (58 living, 2 fossil; habitat Fossorial 21 / Terrestrial 15 / Aquatic 11 / Arboreal 11 / Unknown 2). SD4 data.csv: 1,150 rows = 115 specimens x 10 measurement points along a bone, 66 columns, burrowing-lifestyle codes in 0/1 columns.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: SD2 phylogeny content (166 taxa x 394 morphological characters, 95-taxon 11-locus molecular set) is from the README only; not downloaded. The raw micro-CT scans and meshes sit on MorphoSource (project 000780586), not checked.

a1_downloadable.note: Dataverse files open and download without login under a CC0 licence; checked.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Habitat class is a column in SPECIES_CLASSIFIERS.csv and burrowing codes are columns in data.csv; checked in the files.

a3_inputs_present.note: 3D landmark coordinates and bone-structure measurements are in the files themselves; checked.

a4_units_stated.note: Landmarks are raw scan coordinates and bone measurements are mostly lengths and ratios; there is no units column, but shape analysis rescales everything anyway, so this is minor.

a5_enough_rows.note: The unit is the species or specimen: 60 species for brain shape and 115 specimens for bone structure (the 1,150 rows are 10 positions per specimen), checked in the files. That is far under the ~400 needed even for classification.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: 60 landmark files match the 60 classifier rows; not cross-checked against the paper's figure legends.

a8_label_provenance.note: Habitat labels come from literature natural-history sources (cited in sample_lifestyle.xlsx), not from a model, though they are coarse expert categories.

integration.partner_dataset: MorphoSource scans or SquamBase-style lifestyle databases (not checked)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Could brain or bone shape predict lifestyle across all squamates (lizards and snakes) if scaled up from many more scanned specimens? That would need new landmarking work, not this dataset.

controls.positive_control: Burrowing living species should cluster apart from non-burrowing ones (the paper's own result).

honest_claim_h3: With 60 species and 4 habitat classes, a model could at most re-state the paper's discriminant analysis of front-brain shape against lifestyle, not learn a general predictor.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use 3D front-brain shape or bone inner structure to predict whether a lizard or snake lives burrowing, on land, in trees or in water.
plain_idea.train_on: Six 3D landmark points on the front brain for 60 species, or bone-density profiles for 115 specimens (both counts checked in the files).
plain_idea.predict: Habitat class (burrowing, terrestrial, tree-dwelling, aquatic), taken from published natural-history records.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Inferring how fossil animals lived from their anatomy is a central question in palaeontology, but this sample is far too small for ML to add anything beyond the authors' own statistics.

ml_idea: Classify squamate habitat from front-brain landmark shape (60 species) or bone microstructure (115 specimens). This is too small for ML; phylogenetic discriminant analysis, which the paper already does, is the right tool.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from file sizes checked in the download; nothing was timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the species or specimens with labels: 60 and 115, done. This kills the project.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 (enough data): the brain-shape set has only 60 species, 2 of them fossils, and the bone set has 115 specimens (both checked in the open CC0 Dataverse files). That is far too few for ML, and the paper's phylogenetic discriminant analysis already covers the task.
